title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning and Runbooks - Standards
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single source of truth for production reliability practices and is required reading for service owners, on-call engineers, and product teams that ship user-facing functionality.

1) SLO & Error Budget Policy

- Purpose: Ensure user-facing quality is quantified and managed; provide clear actions when reliability degrades.
- Measurement windows: primary window = 28-day rolling; secondary window = 7-day rolling for short-term alerts.

Canonical SLOs (examples):
- Availability: 99.95% success rate (external HTTP 2xx) measured on the 28-day rolling window.
- Latency: p99 < 300ms for interactive API requests (business-critical paths).
- Throughput: 99% of requests served at configured concurrency quota without queueing >100ms.
- Embedding job completion: 99.9% complete within configured batch SLA (30s).

Error budget definitions and burn actions:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO over 28-days.
- Burn rate monitoring: use Datadog/Prometheus SLO burn_rate metric.
- Thresholds and actions (automated & human):
  1. Normal: burn_rate < 1 \u2014 continue normal operations.
  2. Elevated: burn_rate between 1 and 2 over 24h \u2014 SRE lead notified, prepare mitigations; throttle non-critical background jobs, pause non-essential rollouts.
  3. High: burn_rate between 2 and 4 over 12h OR over 24h \u2014 immediate mandatory mitigations: revert recent canary, enforce stricter caching, increase instance count if safe.
  4. Critical: burn_rate > 4 in any 1h window \u2014 page SRE on-call, run incident playbook, consider capacity-based limiters and global throttles.

Notes:
- All burn-rate actions and state changes must be recorded in the SLO incident timeline (Datadog event + incident ticket).
- Product teams must include a rollback criterion in release notes tied to error budget state.

2) Capacity Planning Standards

Goals: maintain headroom to absorb expected growth and unplanned spikes, ensure predictable latency under target load, and support fast scaling for Dedicated/Private deployments.

Forecasting cadence and inputs:
- Quarterly capacity review: forecast demand (Q \u2192 Q+2) using usage growth, new features, and contract commitments. Owner: SRE + Capacity PM.
- Monthly run-rate checks: compare actual utilization against forecast; update autoscale policies if sustained delta >10%.
- Inputs: request TPS, p50/p99 latencies, token/sec for generation workloads, prefix-cache hit rates, KV cache occupancy, and model memory footprints.

Headroom policies:
- Minimum operating headroom: 25% spare GPU/instance capacity for Hosted tier during business hours; 40% for Dedicated SLAs during peak.
- Burst capacity: maintain cold-start capacity to absorb 2x baseline spike for up to 15 minutes; enable fast autoscale up to 3x sustained for 30 minutes if budgeted.

Sizing and cost tradeoffs:
- Use load-modeling harness (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) to validate batch sizes and sequence-length distributions.
- For quantized models, track memory overheads and prefer memory-limited autoscale triggers.

3) Reliability Initiatives & Prioritization

Types of initiatives:
- Infrastructure: autoscaler improvements, faster instance provisioning, kernel optimizations.
- Product: degrade-gracefully UX, cache-first paths, background retries.
- Observability: synthetic traffic for critical paths, SLO-derived dashboards, end-to-end tracing for model calls.

Prioritization framework: impact \u00d7 probability \u00d7 detectability (business impact in dollars or customer count) with mandatory inclusion of effort estimate and rollback mitigations. Quarterly reliability roadmap must include at least one initiative aligned to reducing error budget burn.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortem, RCA, and Follow-ups)

Postmortem requirements (for all Sev2+ incidents and Sev3 incidents that hit SLO burn thresholds):
- Title, incident window, severity, impacted services/customers.
- Timeline with timestamps (UTC), evidence (logs/metrics), and actions taken.
- Root cause analysis: avoid blame, include causal chain and contributing factors.
- Corrective actions: immediate, short-term (within 7 days), medium-term (30\u201390 days) with owners and due dates.
- Metrics: quantify user impact (requests, errors, revenue exposure) and error budget consumption.
- Lessons learned and verification plan (how will we validate the fix?).

Postmortem cadence: draft within 48 hours of incident mitigation; final published within 10 business days. All postmortems must be tagged and linked to the incident ticket.

Blameless culture: focus on systemic fixes. If human error occurred, identify tooling/process changes to prevent recurrence (e.g., safer rollout gates, pre-flight checks).

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Minimum observability surface for any service:
- SLO dashboard (28-day and 7-day windows) showing success rate, burn rate, and error-class breakdowns.
- Latency histogram (p50/p95/p99) with heatmap by endpoint and model variant.
- Capacity dashboard: cluster utilization, GPU memory pressure, queue depths, autoscaler actions.
- Synthetic checks: end-to-end synthetic for critical journeys (heartbeat every 1 minute).
- Alerting: only actionable alerts; use aggregated alerts for noisy signals.

Alerting policy examples (Datadog/Prometheus):
- SLO burn rate > 1.5 over 24h: notify SRE lead and product owner (pagerduty + slack).
- p99 latency > 500ms sustained for 10 minutes: page on-call.
- Cluster GPU memory pressure > 80% for 15 minutes: page infra on-call.

Tooling stack (preferred):
- Metrics: Prometheus + remote write to Datadog for dashboards.
- Tracing: Jaeger/Tempo with sample rates tied to error budget state.
- Logs: Elasticsearch cluster with retention tiers.
- Incident management: PagerDuty + internal incident ticketing (Jira).

6) Runbooks (canonical templates and examples)

Runbook structure (required fields):
- Title
- Scope/when to use
- Owner and escalation (pagerduty rotations, Slack channels)
- Pre-reqs (playback creds, query templates, runbook links)
- Step-by-step mitigation procedure (numbered)
- Verification steps and rollback criteria
- Post-incident actions and link to postmortem template

Example Runbook: API High Error Rate (500s)
- Scope: user-facing text-generation API endpoints returning 5xx.
- Owner: api-service-oncall (pagerduty: PD-API-Primary)
- Steps:
  1. Confirm alert: open SLO dashboard, check 28d and 7d windows, inspect error-class tags.
  2. Identify recent deploys: git commit, rollout window, and canary logs. CLI: git log --oneline --since="24 hours"
  3. If deploy suspect: rollback canary via rollout service: curl -X POST https://deploys.internal/api/rollback -d '{\"service\":\"api-service\",\"to\":\"stable\"}' (replace with internal CLI).
  4. If resource pressure suspect: scale up staging instance group by +2 or trigger autoscale override: ./infra autoscale set --group api-prod --min 4 --max 20 --reason "emergency".
  5. If model OOM or timeout: switch to fallback model variant (model-router CLI: model-router promote --variant small-quant --service api-service).
  6. Apply short-term rate limits for non-authenticated routes: update gateway policy (console) and monitor error delta.
  7. Verify: success rate back to baseline for 30 minutes, p99 latency within threshold.
  8. Create incident ticket and attach timeline; start postmortem draft.

Example Runbook: High GPU Memory Pressure
- Scope: cluster-level GPU memory > 80% for >15 minutes.
- Steps:
  1. Check active jobs: prometheus query job_gpu_memory_usage_by_job.
  2. Identify long-running background jobs and pause them: ./jobs pause --job-id <id>.
  3. Evict low-priority batches (batch-id list available in queue UI).
  4. Temporarily increase instance count if autoscale can provision within 5 minutes.
  5. If OOM persists, fall back to quantized model variant and route traffic.

7) Ownership, SLAs and Escalation Paths

- Service owner responsibilities: maintain SLOs, own postmortem, own reliability roadmap items.
- SRE responsibilities: operating runbooks, capacity forecasting, corrective engineering, and performing root cause analyses.
- Escalation path: on-call -> SRE lead -> Eng manager -> Head of Platform. Each step must have a documented SLA for acknowledgement (5m -> 15m -> 60m -> 4h).

8) Governance and Continuous Improvement

- Quarterly SLO review: service owners must justify SLOs, propose changes, and document customer impact.
- SRE-led reliability retro: quarterly meeting to review incident trends, top error-budget consumers, and planned initiatives.
- Automation targets: aim to automate 50% of runbook steps for high-frequency incidents within 12 months.
